name: Brazilian / intimate waxing

card.summary: Wax removal of pubic hair, from a swimsuit-line trim to full removal; common and well documented, with ingrown hairs and folliculitis as the usual complaints.
card.aka: Bikini wax, Hollywood wax, intimate waxing
card.note: Pain, ingrown hairs and follicle infections are reported; skin lifting is more likely with certain medications and conditions.

quick.overview:
Brazilian waxing removes most or all pubic hair using warm or cold wax and cloth strips, or stripless hard wax. Related styles include the American (swimsuit-line) and French (landing strip) waxes. The Brazilian name is traced to a Manhattan salon founded in 1987 by seven Brazilian sisters.

It is mainly associated with women but male waxing has become more common. A 2016 JAMA Dermatology survey of 3,316 US women found 84% reported lifetime pubic hair grooming, 59% citing hygiene as the main reason.
quick.mechanism: Wax grips the hair and pulls it out from the follicle, so regrowth typically takes around four to six weeks. Proponents say repeated waxing can weaken regrowth and make sessions less painful and less frequent.
quick.risks: Pain varies from slight to severe. Bumps and ingrown hairs can last two to five days, and folliculitis has been reported to be rising among women who wax or shave the bikini area. People with weakened immune systems face higher infection risk if waxing is done improperly. Critics also raise cultural objections to full removal.

lead: Brazilian waxing, also called intimate or bikini waxing, is the removal of pubic hair using hot or cold wax pulled off with cloth strips or, in stripless forms, peeled off once hardened.[1][2] Styles range from the American, which removes only the hair a swimsuit would show, through the French, which leaves a vertical strip, to the Brazilian or 'Hollywood', which removes all or nearly all hair.[1]

Prevalence data come from surveys: a 2016 JAMA Dermatology study of 3,316 American women reported that 84% had groomed pubic hair at some point.[1] Reported complications include pain, ingrown hairs, bumps and folliculitis.[1][2] No clinical trial in the sources reviewed has tested Brazilian waxing as an intervention.

paras: In a typical session the area is cleaned and powdered, wax is applied in the direction of hair growth and strips are pulled off against it. Long hair may be trimmed first. Bikini wax is often a beeswax and tall oil blend, described as effective on coarse pubic hair.[1]

Soft or strip wax is spread thinly and removed with a cloth strip, while hard or film wax is applied thicker and peeled off without a strip; hard wax is described as suited to sensitive skin and potentially less painful.[2] A patch test on the upper thigh is recommended in the source to check for allergy, and ibuprofen or topical anaesthetics are mentioned as pain reducers.[1]

Pubic hair removal has been recorded in several cultures: an ethnologist in 1901 observed it as a custom of the Nair caste in India, and in Islam removal of unwanted body hair is regarded as part of fitra, or natural practice.[1] Wikipedia links the rise of the bikini from 1946 and changes in lingerie to greater interest in grooming.[1]

The Brazilian wax was named by the J. Sisters salon in Manhattan, founded in 1987 by seven Brazilian sisters.[1] Some people consider a fully bare result erotic or youthful-looking, while others style or avoid grooming for identity or cost reasons.[1] Critics argue the Brazilian can make adult women appear underage; this is a recorded criticism rather than an established finding.[1]

Pain can range from slight to severe and is generally greater during pregnancy. Bumps and ingrown hairs occur, with discomfort typically lasting two to five days.[1] Wikipedia notes a rise in folliculitis among women who wax or shave the bikini area, and a higher infection risk for people with weakened immune systems if waxing is poorly performed.[1]

Skin lifting is more likely with blood thinners, steroids, drugs for autoimmune disease, topical retinoids, recent sunburn, laser or peels, and conditions such as eczema or psoriasis. Waxing can also trigger cold sores in people with a history of them.[2]
Bikini waxing has been credited with a reduction in pubic lice cases.[1]
No studies found. A 2016 survey study in JAMA Dermatology of 3,316 US women reported prevalence of grooming (84% lifetime) and motivations, but did not test waxing as a treatment.[1]

timeline.event: An ethnologist records pubic hair removal as a custom among the Nair caste in India.[1]
